question: The EU cosmetics industry faces significant costs and complexity in ensuring that products placed on the market meet the stringent safety and environmental standards required by EU legislation. While the same expectations apply to all imported cosmetics, in the absence of proper controls on the quality and conformity of products originating from outside the EU, European industry may face unfair competition, and EU citizens and the EU environment may in addition be exposed to unacceptable risks. 1.

Does the Commission have data on the number of inspections conducted on cosmetics at EU customs checkpoints by the Member States, on the types of inspection carried out and on whether these include thorough analytical investigations so as to exclude the potential presence of prohibited substances and of trace impurities in avoidable concentrations?

Are the number, frequency and types of border inspection representative of the variety of imported cosmetics and their diverse origin, and are they statistically meaningful in terms of providing a clear understanding of the volumes of imported goods in this sector?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Andrey Novakov (PPE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.5.2026) Under Regulation (EC) No 1223/20091, the ‘responsible person’2 must ensure compliance of cosmetics on the EU market, while enforcement, including import controls, is carried out by Member States based on national, risk-based strategies.

Non-compliant products are detained at customs when breaches of compliance are suspected and referred to market surveillance authorities (MSAs) for confirmation. In 2025, the Commission coordinated Priority Control Area actions carried out by customs and MSAs in all 27 Member States, investigating the level of non-compliance of e-commerce consignments, including cosmetics.

Through documentary and laboratory checks, almost 6000 cosmetics were inspected, with an average non-compliance rate of 65%3. The ongoing revision of the Union Customs Code4 aims to strengthen EU customs’ import supervision, including on cosmetics, through a more robust and efficient framework, digital tools and closer cooperation of customs and MSAs.

The Commission’s upcoming proposal on the European Product Act (which revises the Market Surveillance Regulation5) also aims to improve compliance with product rules. While there is no centralised EU inspection system, information on enforcement actions6 is exchanged through the Information Communication System for Market Surveillance7, the Customs Risk Management System8 and the Safety Gate rapid alert system910.

As market surveillance enforcement is organised nationally and risk-based and customs controls are carried out by the national customs authorities, inspections vary across Member States. The Commission therefore does not collect harmonised EU-wide statistics on the number or types of inspections carried out at customs and MSAs on a per product sector basis. 1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?
